list.listitem: Evaluate for primary aldosteronism (PA) in patients with hypertension associated with adrenal incidentaloma, spontaneous or diuretic induced hypokalemia, drug resistant hypertension (three or more drugs required for control), hypertension and sleep apnea, patients with JNC VI hypertension stages 2 or 3, and in patients with hyertension and family history of early onset hypertension or CVA at a young age (<40 years). C

Best initial test is the ratio of plasma aldosterone concentration to plasma renin activity (angiotensin renin ratio or ARR); a positive test is a ratio of more than 20 ng/dL/ng/mL/h usually associated with a PAC more than 15 ng/dL. C
Confirm the diagnosis by additional testing with saline suppression test, oral salt load, fludrocortisone suppression test, or captopril suppression test. C
Once the diagnosis is confirmed, determine whether the cause is unilateral or bilateral adrenal disease. C
Treat with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist if the cause is idiopathic hyperaldosteronism (IHA), if the patient is not a surgical candidate or if the patient declines surgery. A
Treat with adrenalectomy if a unilateral cause of PA is confirmed. B

background.definition: Primary aldosteronism is a group of disorders in which aldosterone production is inappropriately high, relatively autonomous, and non-suppressible by sodium loading.

list.listitem: Mean prevalence of PA is estimated at 4.3% among hypertensive patients in primary care and 9.5% among referred patients with hypertension.
Prevalence increases with worsening hypertension. There is 2% prevalence in stage 1, 8% in stage 2, and 13% in stage 3 hypertension. (stages defined by Joint National Committee VI).

However, the heterogenity of studies aimed at estimating the prevlaence of primary aldosteronism is probably misleading (I(2) = 57.6% for studies in primary care and I(2) = 97.1% in referral centers), casting doubt on published estimates.
The prevalence of PA ranges from 14% to 21% in patients with resistant hypertension.
Patients with untreated PA have a higher risk of CV events, including MI, stroke, and atrial fibrillation than patients with essential hypertension.

In a population of persons without known hyperaldosteronism, higher aldosterone to renin ratio, suggestive of subclinical hyperthyroidism was associated with some physiologic measures of cardiovascular health (higher blood pressure, increased arterial stiffness, and cardiac remodeling.
IHA/bilateral adrenal hyperplasia: 65%.
Aldosterone producing adenoma (APA): 30%.
Primary unilateral adrenal hyperplasia (UAH): 3%.
Aldosterone producing adrenocortical carcinoma: 1%.
Aldosterone producing ovarian tumor: <1%.

Familial hyperaldosteronism type I or glucocorticoid remediable aldosteronism (GRA): <1%. GRA is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait that results in aldosterone secretion being regulated by adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). Typically presents with hypertension early in life and increased prevalence of early cerebrovascular complications.
Familial hyperaldosteronism type II, a familial occurrence of APA or IHA, autosomal dominant: unknown frequency.
Familial hyperaldosteronism type III, autosomal dominant, leading to severe childhood hypertension and massive adrenal hyperplasia: unknown frequency.

Aldosterone is iesreted by cells of adrenal glomerulosa in response to hyperkalemia and stimulation of renin angiotensin system (RAS). Aldosterone increases sodium and chloride reabsorption as well as potassium and hydrogen secretion at the distal nephron.

PA is cahracterised by overproduction of aldosterone by adrenal adrenal glands in a manner relatively autonomous of RAS and non-suppressible by sodium loading. This results in volume expansion, hypertension and hypokalemia.
Excess aldosterone secretion has also been shown to be related to vascular inflammation, myocardial fibrosis, left ventricular hypertrophy and renal damage.

Recently, mutations of the potassium channel gene KCNJ5 affecting channel ion selectivity have been identified in both sporadic adosterone-producing adenomas and familial hyperaldosteronsim type III providing insight into disease mechanism.

Endocrine Society guidelines (2026) conditionally recommend screening for aldosteronism in patients with hypertension. They recommend measuring potassium and the plasma aldosterone to plasma renin activity ratio.

Evaluate for primary aldosteronism (PA) in patients with hypertension associated with adrenal incidentaloma, spontaneous or diuretic induced hypokalemia, drug resistant hypertension (3 or more drugs required for control), patients with JNC VI hypertension stages 2 or 3, and in patients with hyertension and family history of early onset hypertension or CVA at a young age (<40 years).C
The best initial screening test of choice is the ratio of plasma aldosterone concentration to plasma renin activity (ARR).C
If the ARR is positive, confirm the PA diagnosis using saline suppression test, oral salt load, fludrocortisone suppression test, or captopril suppression test. C
Once diagnosis is confirmed, perform additional testing to localize the abnormality.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Cushingoid features with low renin and low aldosterone

list.listitem: The classic presentation of PA is the triad of hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Hypokalemia in particular may cause symptoms if severe such as muscle weakness or intermittent paralysis, but this is uncommon, and most patients are asymptomatic.
Inquire about personal age of onset of hypertension and about a family history of early onest hypertension, early cerebrovascular disease, or PA.
Assess the number and classes of medications required for blood pressure control in each patient.
Recent research shows that less than 40% of patients with PA are hypokalemic.

Evaluate for primary aldosteronism (PA) in patients with hypertension associated with adrenal incidentaloma, spontaneous or diuretic induced hypokalemia, drug resistant hypertension (3 or more drugs required for control), patients with JNC VI hypertension stages 2 or 3, and in patients with hyertension and family history of early onset hypertension or CVA at a young age (<40 years).

The best initial test is the ratio of plasma aldosterone concentration to plasma renin activity (ARR) drawn in the morning with the patient seated after having rested for 15 minutes. Cut-off of a positive ARR ranges is 20 for aldosterone (ng/dl) / plasma renin activity [PRA] (ng/mL/hr) and 70 for aldosterone (pmol/L) / direct renin concentration (mU/mL).

If the ARR is positive but the patient is taking a beta-blocker or alpha agonist (e.g. clonidine) then a false positive is possible. The medications should be stopped and the test repeated in 2 weeks.
False negatives may be caused by underlying hypokalemia, mineralicorticoid antagonists, and diuretics.
When the angiotensin renin ratio (ARR) result is inconclusive or difficult to interpret due to interfering medications or other conditions, it should be repeated under optimal conditions.
Non-dihydrpyridine calcium channel blockers, hydralazine and alpha-blockers have no significant effecton ARR and can be used to control BP while repeating ARR.

Patients with a clearly positive ARR do not require a suppression test and should be treated. This includes patients with clinical features of severe PA including hypokalemia, very low renin (direct renin concentation< 2 mU/L or PRA < 0.2 ng/ml/hr) along with aldosterone > 20 ng/dL. Further evaluation for patients considering surgery includes adrenal CT and adrenal venous sampling.

Those with an intermediate probability of lateralizing PA who are candidates for surgery should have the PA diagnosis confirmed by demonstrating failure of aldosterone to suppress under appropriate conditions (). Currently there is no consensus as to the best confirmatory test to diagnosis PA. The decision as to which test to use is based on the availability of the test and clinical experience with the test.

Once the diagnosis of PA has been confirmed then localize the abnormality through further testing as described in . Adrenal vein sampling is the gold standard for determining if PA is due to unilateral or bilateral disease. A clinical prediction rule found that in PA patients with a typical adrenal adenoma 8mm or more in size with normal contralateral adrenal gland plus either a finding of hypoklaemia or eGFR >100 ml/min/1.73 m2, unilateral PA can be predicted with 100% sensitivity and 53% specificity. The authors conclude that AVS can be avoided in such patients.

Glucocorticoid remediable aldosteronism (GRA) is diagnosed in suspected individuals by a dexamethasone suppression test followed by genetic testing to determine presence of hybrid 11 beta-hydroxylase/aldosterone synthase gene.
See algorithm in .
Treatment of choice for IHA is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (eg, spironolactone).A
Treatment of choice for aldosterone-producing adenoma (APA) or unilateral adrenal hyperplasia (UAH) is adrenalectomy.B
Treat with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) for APA and UAH if patient is not a candidate for surgery or if patient declines surgery.C

For IHA or for patients with aldosterone-producing adenoma (APA) and unilateral adrenal hyperplasia (UAH) who are not candidates for surgery or refuse surgery, the treatment of choice is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA), either spironolactone or eplerenone.
MRAs have been shown to be effective in providing BP control as well as BP independent target organ protection.

Spironolactone, a non-selective MRA is considered a more effective and preferred therapy. Eplerenone, a selective MRA is considered an alternative therapy for patients with undesirable side effects of impotence, gynecomastia, menstrual irregularities or mastodynia observed on spironolactone therapy.
Closely monitor the patient's blood pressure and potassium when initiating therapy with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist to prevent hypotension and hyperkalemia.

For GRA, the treatment of choice is a glucocorticoid to partially suppress ACTH production, thereby decreasing aldosterone production. The lowest possible dose should be used to avoid iatrogenic Cushing's. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists can be used in conjunction with glucocorticoids if needed to control blood pressure.
Dietary sodium intake is directly related to the severity of obstructive sleep apnea in patients with hyperaldosteronism and resistant hypertension.

A novel aldosterone synthase inhibitor called lorundrostat was shown in an RCT (n=200 adults with poorly controlled hypertension) to reduce blood pressure by 3 to 10 more mm Hg than placebo. There are no clinical outcome data.
Treatment of choice for aldosterone-producing adenoma (APA) and UAH is adrenalectomy.

The surgery of choice is a laparoscopic adrenalectomy, if available. Laparoscopic partial adrenalectomy has been shown to as safe and effective and laparascopic total adrenalectomy in cure of patients with APA.
A cure rate of up to 44% has been reported after adrenalectomy. Cure was defined as a patient having blood pressure less than 140/90 mm Hg off all antihypertensives.
Majority of patients experience significant improvement in their BP management with drop in BP and reduction in number of anti-hypertensive medications.

A study of 41 patients following adrenalectomy found the largest drop in blood pressure in the first month post-operatively, with little change after that. The authors suggest that long-term follow-up by the surgical team is not needed.
While BP cure or improvement take up to 6 months following surgery, resolution of hypokalemia is immediate.
Patients need to be monitored closely for hyperkalemia and hypotension postoperatively.

Once a diagnosis of PA is suspected secondary to a positive ARR, consider referring the patient to an endocrinologist, a nephrologist, or a hypertension center for the workup to confirm the diagnosis of PA and to localize the abnormality.

Patients with PA have higher rates of stroke (both ischemic and hemorrhagic), nonfatal myocardial infarction (Odds Ratio = 2.6), atrial fibrillation (OR = 5.0), left ventricular hypertrophy (OR = 2.0), and heart failure (OR = 2.9) as compared with patients with essential hypertension.A
Non-inasive ultrasonograhic and serological indices of Aldosterone induced myocardial fibrosis have been shown to be reversed with adrenalectomy and MR antagonist therapy.C

Patients with PA have increased rates of microalbuminuria and albuminuria as compared with patients with essential hypertension. This has been shown to improve after treatment of PA with adrenalectomy or spironolactone.A

feature.caption: Tests to Confirm Primary Aldosteronism. (Test Preference Is Based on Availability and Clinical Experience with Tests.)
feature.feature_body:
Test How to Perform Positive Result
Saline suppression test Infuse 2 L of normal saline over 4 h with the patient recumbent; check serum potassium and plasma aldosterone at baseline and after infusion. PAC >10 ng/dL (280 ρmol/L) after infusion makes diagnosis very likely. PAC <5 ng/dl makes diagnosis very unlikely. PAC between 5-10 ng/dl is indeterminate result.
Oral salt load Patient follows high-salt diet* for 3 d. On the third day, collect a 24-h urine for aldosterone, sodium, and creatinine or collect a PAC. Check potassium daily during test and replete as needed. 24-h urine aldosterone >12 μg/24h (39 nmol/d) with a 24-h urine sodium of >200 mmol/24h.
Fludrocortisone suppression test Give the patient fludrocortisone 0.1 mg every 6 h along with slow release KCL supplements every 6 hours and sodium 30 mmol 3 times a day along with a high-salt diet for 4 d. Serum K+ should be close to 4 measured 4 times a day. On day 4 at 7 am, measure cortisol and at 10 am, measure PAC, PRA, cortisol, and potassium. Upright PAC at 10 am >6 ng/dL with a PRA <1 ng/mL/h, normal potassium levels, and a serum cortisol at 10 am that is lower than the 7 am value.
Captopril suppression test Give patient 25-50 mg captopril after sitting or standing for 1 hour; Measure PAC and PRA at baseline and 2 h after dose. A non-suppressed PAC and consistently suppressed PRA indicates PA. (Substantial false negatives or equivocal results reported).
Abbreviations: PAC, plasma aldosterone concentration; PRA, plasma renin activity. References: (see text).

feature.caption: Tests to Localize Abnormality Resulting in Primary Hyperaldosteronism.
feature.feature_body:
Test Details/How to Perform Findings in APA Findings in IAH Equivocal Results
CT of adrenals With IV contrast, using 2-3-mm slices through the adrenals A well-delineated, single adrenal nodule with a normal contralateral gland is suggestive of APA. Absence of adrenal nodules is suggestive of IHA. If bilateral nodules are seen or if there is a nodule with an abnormal-appearing contralateral gland.
MRI of adrenals Can be used in patients with contraindication to IV contrast. Same as for CT. Same as for CT. Same as for CT.
Postural testing Check a supine PAC at 8 am; have patient maintain an erect posture for 4 h and recheck PAC at noon. A decrease in PAC after 4 h of erect posture is a positive test, consistent with APA. A rise in aldosterone after 4 h of erect posture is a negative test; this is more consistent with IHA, but may be seen in APA or UAH. Has been found to have high rate of false negatives for APA and poor diagnostic accuracy.
Adrenal vein sampling Is a technically difficult study, which requires cannulation of the right and left adrenal veins with measurements of PAC and cortisol (C) from each vein and the periphery; can be performed with ACTH stimulation. An adrenal vein to peripheral cortisol ratio >5 signifies successful cannulation. A lateralization ratio(a) >4 with with continuous cosyntropin stimulation is consistent with APA or UAH. A lateralization ratio <3 with continuous cosyntropin stimulation is consistent with IAH. A lateralization ratio of between 3 and 4.
Abbreviations: ACTH, adrenocorticotropic hormone; APA, aldosterone-producing adenoma; IHA, idiopathic hyperaldosteronism; PAC, plasma aldosterone concentration; UAH, unilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Lateralization ratio = high-side adrenal vein PAC/C divided by low-side adrenal vein PAC/C. References:
